item.title: Jalen Rose Recruits Sada Baby & Detroit Diamond For ‘Pop The Trunk’
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Jalen Rose gives Detroit rap a regular seat on 'Pop the Trunk,' pairing Sada Baby and Detroit Diamond with his new show.
item.content:encoded:
Jalen Rose is bringing Sada Baby and Detroit Diamond into his next show as recurring guests, giving Detroit rap a regular place in Pop the Trunk. The series starts in January with two episodes each week on YouTube and audio platforms.

Same Page Entertainment announced the show Monday, with filming based at its new downtown Detroit studio. Rose founded the company with Detroit Pistons owner Tom Gores, and the format includes interviews, live performances, animation and comedy sketches.

“At its core, Pop the Trunk is about creating the kind of conversations that happen when great stories, different viewpoints, and authentic personalities come together,” said Jalen Rose, Co-Founder and CEO of Same Page Entertainment. “We’re opening the door to something entirely new at Same Page and building something entertaining, unpredictable, and rooted in community. Filming in Detroit is especially meaningful because this city shaped who I am, and we’re excited to showcase its talent and resilience on a global stage.”

The company also plans material between episodes, including behind-the-scenes content and social media commentary.

Detroit Diamond already has experience making her music work for television audiences. She reached the final four of Netflix’s Rhythm + Flow alongside Jay Taj, Sura Ali and eventual winner DreTL during the competition’s second season.

Her single “Pressure,” performed during that run, was released in December 2024. That season put contestants through battles, group challenges and live performances before judges Ludacris, DJ Khaled and Latto.

Rose’s own podcast history stretches back to the Grantland years, when his partnership with David Jacoby began in 2011. Their operation later combined television with additional podcast-only material, recorded before the daily TV show for listeners who wanted more personal conversations. Their television setup occupied a smaller podcast room rather than ESPN’s larger studios.

His Detroit connections also extend to education, a commitment that prompted Ice Cube to select him for the 2025 Ice Cube Impact Award. Rose founded the tuition-free Jalen Rose Leadership Academy in 2011, with college preparation central to the school’s work.

Sada Baby has already appeared in another project from Rose’s company. He was among the guest performers in South West High, whose music team included Royce 5’9″ and Denaun Porter.

Same Page’s earlier projects include the Tubi series South West High. The company has also finished production on its first feature, The Streak, a basketball comedy starring Ed Helms.

The new show’s recurring segments will include “Story Time with Jalen Rose.”

item.title: Yung Joc Says Authorities Contact Him Over Massive $4.6M Snap Fraud Connected To Shawty Dred
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Yung Joc explains why he stepped forward after authorities reached out about his appearances alongside Shawty Dred.
item.content:encoded:
Yung Joc says authorities contacted him after videos with Shawty Dred drew attention, prompting him to publicly explain their connection.

The Atlanta rapper addressed the footage in an interview with Atlanta News First Investigates, saying he wanted to clear his name.

“Hell no, I didn’t know what he was doing,” Yung Joc said when asked about the influencer’s activities. He described boarding a private jet for a skit, without a script or a planned destination, and said he never flew with Shawty Dred.

Joc said their association stretched back around 20 years, but he eventually stopped working with him over conflicts involving other people. He also challenged Vice President JD Vance’s joking treatment of the case, arguing that the allegations deserved a serious response.

“I never seen him do it, but I saw the money,” Joc said while discussing the accusations.

The rapper said people had reached out because of the videos and stressed that he didn’t want any connection to fraudulent activity. Atlanta News First reported that the indictment doesn’t name Joc as a defendant.

Shawty Dred’s 63-count federal indictment dates to October 7, with his arrest following October 13 in Las Vegas. Prosecutors allege he controlled more than 350 SNAP accounts opened with stolen identities between January 2020 and July 2026.

The alleged scheme involved roughly $4.6 million transferred into those accounts, with about $4 million taken out.

Prosecutors say his company obtained authorization to accept SNAP payments, then used fraudulently obtained benefit cards and a payment device to collect more than $660,000.

That retailer authorization was revoked in November 2025, according to the federal account of the case. About two weeks afterward, police seized 14 cards issued to other people during an arrest over alleged benefit sales, and prosecutors say replacement cards were subsequently mailed to Atlanta-area addresses.

The charges include mail fraud, aggravated identity theft, SNAP fraud and illegal access-device transactions, and Shawty Dred remains presumed innocent. The October announcement said he was held in U.S. Marshals custody pending further proceedings.

Joc also said his morning radio show will mark its 10th anniversary on December 10.

item.title: Scarface Says He No Longer Wants To Release Records
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Scarface opens up about his creative frustration as Roxanne Shante urges the Houston legend to keep his musical fire alive.
item.content:encoded:
Scarface says he’s lost the desire to write and release records, opening up about a painful disconnect from the work that made him a Hip-Hop giant.

The Houston rapper discussed those feelings in a Paid In Full Foundation conversation released November 10. Roxanne Shante had praised the emotional honesty of “I Seen a Man Die” when he explained how differently he feels about creating now.

“I don’t even want to write no more. I don’t even want to put no records out no more,” Scarface said.

He expressed concern about someone else releasing new music he makes, without identifying that person. Shante encouraged him to keep creating and lean on the support around him.

His catalog stretches from the Geto Boys to a solo run that began with Mr. Scarface Is Back in 1991. The Diary followed in 1994, carrying “I Seen a Man Die,” while 2002’s The Fix brought collaborations with Jay-Z and Nas.

Scarface has wrestled publicly with leaving rap before. In 2022, he announced a farewell tour with his band, Formaldehyde Funkmen, following a sold-out Houston show. The itinerary included a stop at LL Cool J’s Rock the Bells festival in Queens.

At the time, his interests extended beyond rap into blues, rock and alternative music. His plans followed serious health challenges: he tested positive for COVID-19 in March 2020 and suffered kidney failure, requiring dialysis.

In September 2021, his son Christopher Jordan donated a kidney to him. Christopher reported afterward that the surgery had gone well and that his father’s new kidney was working. The transplant came nearly a year after Scarface publicly sought a donor.

His later performances also showed how much room remained inside the catalog. NPR released his Tiny Desk Concert in December 2023, with Mike Dean on keys and Scarface handling vocals and guitar.

The six-song set moved between solo material and the Geto Boys, including “On My Block,” “Smile” and “Mind Playing Tricks on Me.” “I Seen a Man Die” was also part of that performance, connecting the song Shante singled out to his work with a live band.

Another health crisis followed in 2024. On October 8 that year, Scarface revealed on Instagram that he had undergone open-heart surgery six weeks earlier, sharing his gratitude for being alive.

Scarface and Rakim were the Paid In Full Foundation’s inaugural honorees in 2023.

item.title: Big Boi Says Fatherhood Finally Wins Him Over To Podcasting
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Big Boi teams with Bamboo and Cross for candid family discussions after spending years resisting his manager's podcast pitch.
item.content:encoded:
Big Boi needed a reason to become a podcaster, and his sons finally gave him one after a decade of pitches. The OutKast rapper is putting fatherhood at the center of “Big Boi’s Bloodlines & Basslines,” with Bamboo and Cross joining him behind the microphones.

His manager had pushed the idea for 10 years, Big Boi told The Atlanta Journal-Constitution in an interview. A famous name wasn’t enough to make him want the job.

“It’s got to be about something,” Big Boi said. “It got to mean something.”

The turning point came when Cross interviewed his dad at last year’s Stankonia 25th-anniversary celebration at Cascade Skating Rink. That conversation gave Big Boi a format he could get behind: talking with his own children about fatherhood.

The show debuted November 11 through iHeartPodcasts, with three installments planned each week. Recorded in Atlanta, the series gives the family room to disagree, tell stories and compare experiences across generations.

“This podcast is me and my two sons chopping it up about life, family and everything in between,” said Big Boi. “We’re talking about the things we love, the places we’ve been, the lessons we’ve learned, and where we’re headed next. Y’all know me from the music, but this is a chance to see another side of me, just being Dad and having real conversations with my boys. At the end of the day, the music is part of my legacy, but what I pass down to my sons means everything. Cross and Bamboo are the future, and I’m here to make sure they’re ready to carry that torch. And with iHeart’s reach, we get to bring these conversations to families and listeners all over the world.”

Bamboo comes to those conversations as a father himself, while Cross brings experience as a former Division I football player. Both have interests beyond their dad’s recording career, including business and real estate.

The premiere, “Raised Right,” gets into Big Boi becoming a father at 19 and the rules his children grew up with. Its episode description lists schoolwork taking priority over gaming and a household where their father’s success didn’t erase expectations.

There’s family history in the mix, too, including a $10,000 phone bill and a childhood stay at Hank Aaron’s pool house. The episode also examines how Big Boi balanced affection with discipline while raising his children.

The November 13 follow-up, “Turn Up Tunes,” moves into the family’s musical tastes. Its episode notes also promise a discussion of how Big Boi sought his children’s reactions when deciding which tracks should become singles.

The family has already recorded more than 50 episodes, according to the AJC interview. Sessions happen on Tuesdays, either at Stankonia Studios or in Big Boi’s basement.

Big Boi also supplies the show’s original music.

item.title: Kenzo B Explains Why Motherhood Helped Her Leave Drill Behind
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Kenzo B explains why she's leaving drill behind, how motherhood changed her priorities and what she's planning next.
item.content:encoded:
Kenzo B doesn’t want to keep rapping about a life she’s moved beyond, and motherhood helped her decide to leave it behind. The Bronx artist explained her departure from drill in a November 15 interview with Gabe P on On The Radar’s The Frequency, describing a different direction for her music.

“Like I feel like I’ll be disgusted if I did a drill song right now,” Kenzo B said. She explained that she’d started moving away from that mindset before becoming a mother, and her son’s arrival reinforced the change.

Her early catalog includes “Bump It,” which sampled Dick Dale, and “The Realest,” both released while she was still in high school. She developed her writing alongside her brother Bando, competing at home over borrowed beats before bringing her own songs to listeners.

Kenzo named “DeadGame” as her last drill song and said she’d already been questioning that direction when she released it. She still listens to drill records she enjoys, but said she no longer wants to rap about that lifestyle herself.

“DeadGame” arrived through Coke Boys/Warner Records in March 2023, following her debut mixtape, Top Dawg, in 2022. That project included “Hood Love Story,” while “BFFR” followed in June 2023, extending a run of releases under the same label partnership.

She followed Top Dawg with the six-track Top 2, Not 2, which included “Chapters,” “Disrespectful” and “N.B.L.” That mixtape also carried “BFFR” alongside “Gotta Go” and “Get Got.”

For her return, Kenzo said she’s trying to balance what she wants to say with the sounds listeners expect. She also wants to deliver music consistently after spending time away, telling Gabe, “I’m not going to disappear, y’all.”

She said she’s working toward another project, but doesn’t think an album is the right immediate move for artists in her position.

Her collaborations have included an appearance on Sha Gz’s RUTHLESS GZ, whose track “Cheeks” featured Kenzo. She also joined 2Rare and DJ Smallz 732 on the remix of Zeddy Will’s “You,” expanding her recorded collaborations beyond her own solo releases.

Her latest On The Radar freestyle, “back on the radar,” reached streaming services on November 2 under On The Radar Records.

item.title: Missy Elliott Clears Up “Work It” Lyric Confusion With Radio Edit Explanation
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Missy Elliott settles a "Work It" lyric question and explains the extra studio sessions behind the song's clean radio version.
item.content:encoded:
Missy Elliott explained why a familiar line in “Work It” sounds different on its radio-friendly recording after a listener questioned whether their memory of the song was wrong.

The exchange began with an X user pointing out that they heard “chacha” where they remembered “chocha.” The listener described the discrepancy as a Mandela effect, prompting Missy to identify the recording as the clean version.

Missy said making those recordings required another trip into the studio. Rather than simply leaving the original wording in place, artists recorded replacement language for radio airplay.

In her November 15 response on X, Missy explained, “you had to replace dirty or curse words with clean words so it could play on the radio.”

The clarification arrived during the anniversary week of Under Construction, the album that introduced “Work It.” Released November 12, 2002, the project followed Miss E… So Addictive and became her fourth studio album.

“Work It” has another studio story behind its unusual vocals. In a 2018 Associated Press interview, Missy recalled that an engineer accidentally played part of the recording backward. She liked how the reversed passage landed against the beat and decided to build her writing around it.

“The reverse thing, that was a mistake,” Missy said in that earlier interview. She also recalled taking several attempts at the song before Timbaland approved the version that became the record.

For those sessions, Missy said she worked in a separate room because she did not record with other people watching. Timbaland’s approval came around her fifth attempt, she recalled.

Missy has previously discussed how studio disagreements shaped her catalog, including pushing Timbaland to keep working on “Get Ur Freak On” when she felt her preceding album still needed another song. That track arrived a year before Under Construction.

The Recording Academy awarded “Work It” Best Female Rap Solo Performance in 2004. Its fellow nominees included records by Da Brat, Lil’ Kim, MC Lyte and Queen Latifah, while Under Construction also received an Album of the Year nomination.

Missy later performed “Work It” with Mary Halsey on Ellen after Halsey’s karaoke rendition spread online in 2018.

item.title: Marshawn Lynch Takes Ownership Stake In Black Pharo Cognac
item.dc:creator: Houston Williams
item.description: Marshawn Lynch has a fresh entrepreneurial chapter with Black Pharo cognac, a championship push for an American liquor rollout.
item.content:encoded:
Marshawn Lynch has joined Black Pharo Cognac as a co-owner and equity partner to support the French spirits brand’s expansion across the United States.

The retired NFL running back and Super Bowl champion became an equity partner in the company recently, but it was not announced until late October.

His investment gives the partnership a financial foundation beyond a mere celebrity endorsement now that Black Pharo seeks additional retail shelves and distribution.

The company did not disclose the size or value of Lynch’s ownership stake.

“Everyone knows I have an exquisite palate when it comes to ‘yack.’ So when I had my first taste, I was like okay… I’m f’n with it,” said Lynch. “Then I learned more about the product, the team and the vision, took a second to slow down and learn about the history of cognac and why it is what it is and does what it does.”

Black Pharo currently has distribution in Texas and Georgia. Nevada and Washington state are its next priority markets. California is in their immediate sights for expansion. Texas retailers carrying the cognac include Spec’s Wine, Spirits & Finer Foods and Total Wine & More.

The company says it intends to establish retail and distributor relationships before increasing broader consumer marketing.

“Black Pharo has its own story and something a little different to bring to the table,” Lynch continued. “I’m always looking for new ways to build, give back, bring people together… Black Pharo is something I believe in for hella reasons, and this is an opportunity to be part of something from the ground floor. We’re putting folks on notice and ready to brick by brick this thing into something that lasts.”

Spirits industry veterans Patrick Charpentier and Jerome Hyafil founded the brand.

Charpentier previously held a sales and marketing leadership position at Rémy Cointreau and helped create A. de Fussigny and NYAK cognacs. Hyafil previously served as Seagram’s chief manufacturing officer.

“Marshawn represents exactly the kind of energy and authenticity we envisioned for Black Pharo,” said Patrick Charpentier. “He is not simply lending his name to a product. He believes in what we are building, from the quality of the cognac to the story behind the brand. Together, we have an opportunity to introduce something distinctive to an established category and build a brand with lasting cultural and commercial relevance.”

Black Pharo takes its inspiration from ancient Egypt’s Twenty-fifth Dynasty, also called the Nubian or Black Pharaoh Dynasty.

Its flagship VS cognac is bottled at 84 proof and aged at least two years in French oak. According to the company, it received a 94-point rating from The Tasting Panel.

Lynch’s brother Maurice Sapp, a strategic partnerships representative for Beast Mode, helped arrange the agreement.

item.title: DJ Premier, Masta Ace & Hip-Hop Mourn eMC’s Stricklin, Who Leaves Behind Remarkable Legacy
item.dc:creator: Houston Williams
item.description: Stricklin inspired heartfelt farewells as Premier, Masta Ace and others recollect the admired MC’s devotion to lyrical craftsmanship and civic duty.
item.content:encoded:
Beloved eMC rapper Stricklin earned international respect on Hip-Hop stages while serving Milwaukee as a firefighter before his death Nov. 11 at 56.

The rapper known as Strick and Big Strick left behind recordings with Masta Ace and eMC alongside a career in public service. His death prompted tributes recognizing the artist who represented Milwaukee far beyond Wisconsin. A cause of death has not been publicly disclosed.

DJ Premier acknowledged both sides of that life in an Instagram tribute.

“R.I.P. My Dude! Stricklin you put it down for HIP HOP and the Milwaukee Fire Dept.”

Masta Ace, who has one of the closest relationships with the rapper, paid tribute to Stricklin on Facebook by sharing photographs and videos of their time together. The former Juice Crew king included memories from international travels and performances.

Ace described the difficulty of processing a loss that reached beyond their musical partnership. Four days ago, he said he had no words at all.

“I have so many memories with Steve Stricklin to share… this was Chicago 2018…. I will miss sharing the stage with him.., im still compiling my full thoughts… i need more time. Because it aint just about music…. It never was.”

The collection offered a personal look at their years together, preserving moments from a friendship Ace was still finding the words to honor.

For AllHipHop readers, Stricklin’s story also lives in an archive documenting the relationships behind his music. Years before these farewells, his collaborators described a connection that reached beyond recording sessions.

In a March 2008 AllHipHop interview, Masta Ace explained how touring and repeated collaborations helped bring Stricklin, Punchline and Wordsworth together as eMC.

“It’s not just about the music with us, we are pretty much like brothers.”

Ace said audience enthusiasm helped encourage the group’s formation after listeners repeatedly watched the artists perform together. Their chemistry had developed through shared travel and work rather than a label assembling recognizable names.

AllHipHop witnessed that partnership in action.

An April 2008 Atlanta concert review documented Stricklin joining Ace for “Unfriendly Game,” a song connecting football imagery with social problems. The review also described members stepping away during songs featuring other performers, giving each artist room to command the stage. Stricklin had his own place within the collective.

The group’s debut album, The Show, arrived in 2008. AllHipHop’s review examined its stories about touring, relationships and even the frustrations of performing.

When eMC signed with Penalty Entertainment and Sony RED in 2014, label executive Neil Levine praised the members’ commitment.

“I’m honored to be working with eMC. These guys are amazing lyricists and true to the art form,” Levine said in a statement reported by AllHipHop.

The group followed with The Turning Point EP and The Tonite Show. Stricklin also continued collaborating with Ace and Marco Polo, including on “Life Music” with Speech and E Smitty.

Marco Polo’s farewell returned to the experiences behind those records.

“I’m grateful I got to be there for your wedding. We toured the world together.”

Stricklin’s career connected a hometown commitment with a life of international performance. The records preserve his voice. AllHipHop’s earlier reporting preserves something else: the friendships, shared stages and mutual respect that gave those records their foundation.

item.title: Sexyy Red Reveals Why Drake Is Her Go-To For Advice
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Sexyy Red explains why she turns to Drake for guidance and tells DJ Holiday what she wants from her next relationship.
item.content:encoded:
Sexyy Red says Drake is the person she calls when the music business leaves her with questions, describing a friendship built on advice and records.

The St. Louis rapper discussed their connection during DJ Holiday’s interview for Hot 107.9.

Asked what Drake taught her about business and music, she said she brings him situations she doesn’t understand.

“Like what’s this? What’s going on? He’ll tell me. He’ll give me the real,” Sexyy Red said.

Holiday also asked whether the closeness surprised her, bringing up online speculation about the pair dating. Sexyy Red acknowledged that Drake’s stature still gives her pause, even as she expressed confidence in her own personality.

“I ain’t surprised, but I mean a little bit I am. It’s Drake,” Sexyy Red said.

Their work together stretches back to her appearance on Drake’s It’s All a Blur Tour. She later joined him and SZA on “Rich Baby Daddy,” which appeared on his 2023 album For All the Dogs.

Drake returned the favor with a feature on “U My Everything,” released on her 2024 project In Sexyy We Trust. Their public friendship has also drawn outside commentary: Sexyy Red previously responded to Joe Budden’s speculation about Drake promoting her music.

In the new conversation, she described herself as a reliable friend and explained why people who know her would understand their bond. Holiday then shifted from Drake to her dating life, asking who she was seeing.

“Nobody,” Sexyy Red replied. She said she wanted a partner who could meet her standards rather than a relationship that left them struggling to connect.

“I need somebody that’s on my level,” Sexyy Red said.

The interview also covered her recent performance with Usher and Chris Brown, including the nerves she still experiences before stepping onstage. She told Holiday that she had removed her heels because they made dancing and moving around more difficult.

Sexyy Red also said marriage could be part of her future: “Oh, yeah. I will get married, but not right now. That’s later in life.”

item.title: J Noa Wins First Latin Grammy With Trooko For “Antisistema”
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: J Noa turns four straight nomination years into a breakthrough trophy as her collaboration with Trooko earns Latin Grammy gold.
item.content:encoded:
J Noa has her first Latin Grammy after four consecutive years of nominations, winning Best Rap/Hip Hop Song with Trooko for “Antisistema.” The November 12 victory in Las Vegas rewards a record built around resisting pressure to fit somebody else’s formula.

The Latin Recording Academy’s official results list the pair as winners in the songwriting category. Their competition included “El Pana Deiby,” “Gohan y Goku,” “Mono” and “Poder,” a field stretching across several corners of Spanish-language rap.

For the Dominican rapper, the trophy follows a run that started with “Autodidacta” in 2023. Her team’s announcement traces the next nominations through “Cabecear” in 2024 and “Sudor y Tinta,” alongside Vakero, in 2025.

“Antisistema” arrived in May, months before the awards ceremony. Her representatives describe the track as a challenge to music-industry expectations and commercial templates, with J Noa insisting on room to develop without abandoning her identity.

That position predates this particular win. In a June 2023 interview with People Chica about her debut EP, she pushed back against the idea that rap belonged to men and encouraged Black listeners not to let prejudice limit their ambitions. She described that first project as a test of her songwriting, a process that helped her see possibilities beyond the obstacles.

“I also want them to understand that being Black is not a reason to stop a dream,” J Noa told the publication.

Her account of learning to rap begins closer to home than an awards stage. Speaking with Viper in May 2024, she credited neighborhood freestylers performing outside her house with sparking her interest, rather than pointing to one famous artist.

She also described a writing routine that follows ideas instead of a schedule, stopping other activities to capture a line when inspiration arrives. Asked what success meant, J Noa answered: “Feeling good about what I’m doing, making my family happy and being well mentally.”

The ceremony also featured Janet Jackson’s presentation to Daddy Yankee, recognizing another generation of Latin urban music. J Noa’s award adds a first-time winner’s milestone to that same week’s celebration.

The Academy has released J Noa and Trooko’s acceptance video on its official website.
